findings.impact: High for a developer deciding whether to integrate: the concept describes the intended data relationship but leaves the actual entrypoint and integration surface unknown.
findings.observation: The DEX case is explicitly illustrative. The developer disclosure lists existing source README commands but says they were not run by the page, and labels Web assembly and transaction commands as future proposals.
findings.evidence: Explorer case “Batched DEX orders”; Developer journey disclosures “Current source commands & proposed interfaces” and “A useful developer handoff.”
findings.suggestedChange: Add a direct link to the current developer README and a small status-tagged DEX handoff showing the first supported command or API, its input/output artifacts, and the first unsupported boundary. If no supported DEX path exists, label the case as a target workflow before the CTA.

findings.impact: Medium: I can understand the target idea, but cannot turn it into an integration task from this page.
findings.observation: The DEX description says to connect exact assets and minimum net receipt to a specified pool transition, but shows no concrete interface example. The page does give a useful conceptual chain: claim specification, statement, Strand, consuming script.
findings.evidence: Web Explorer intro and selected Batched DEX orders case; Developer journey workflow.
findings.suggestedChange: Show one compact, explicitly illustrative mapping from a DEX order’s input fields to the stated claim/Strand/consumer roles, with each unavailable runtime hook labeled. Keep it clearly separate from a supported SDK recipe.

findings.impact: Low: the main CTA can read like an app entrypoint on first glance.
findings.observation: The hero button says “Explore a Web”; the same hero immediately qualifies the page as an interactive concept illustration and says integration and settlement are unestablished. Later labels and caveats are clear.
findings.evidence: Desktop and mobile top screenshots; hero text immediately below the CTA; explorer screenshot labels the content illustrative.
findings.suggestedChange: Consider “Explore the Web illustration” or add a short “concept walkthrough” label to the CTA so the interactive surface is identified before click.

findings.impact: A wallet integrator could mistake the worksheet's 2 CASH program fee for the complete fee burden, because network costs are separate but only named in a deeper disclosure.
findings.observation: The worksheet presents gross escrow debit as payment plus 2 CASH fee. The Duties, backing and fees disclosure later says a program-asset fee is not a network fee and identifies network fees, collateral, claim-output min-ADA and thread reserve as separate funding items. No network fee amount is calculated.
findings.evidence: Worksheet visible labels Program fee and Gross escrow debit; collapsed Duties, backing and fees disclosure; viewed live screenshot wallet-proposed-policy.png.
findings.suggestedChange: Add a compact wallet-facing amount breakdown next to gross debit: payment, application/program fee, network fee (not estimated here), and total known/unknown outgoing amount. Keep the separate asset/unit and uncertainty visible.

findings.impact: The intended owner consent may be read as a capability of the current prototype even though the relevant explanation is a collapsed source reading and no genuine intent signature is observed.
findings.observation: The homepage clearly says no signatures or transactions run. The owner-intent fields and approved=true interpretation appear only after opening Effects, allocation and authority; that text labels itself V2 SOURCE READING and says no genuine intent signature is observed.
findings.evidence: Top page scope text; Effects, allocation and authority disclosure text. The same page labels the explorer role as planned and says actual signatures and validator enforcement remain separate.
findings.suggestedChange: Add a short wallet-consent explainer near the worksheet or maturity note, labeled as a design/source reading, with the fields an owner would review and a direct statement that the current page has no signing flow.

findings.impact: A wallet integrator needs to communicate residual duties alongside outgoing amounts; the worksheet already does this clearly for the selected partial.
findings.observation: At 35 CASH the worksheet shows invoice duty 65, reserve duty 10, total duties 75, and says only the payment discharges invoice duty. The proposed 112 CASH funding matches this one partial, while lifecycle text says later partials need another fee allowance and the reserve duty persists after finish.
findings.evidence: Worksheet totals and gross-debit note; Exact asset, opening costs & lifecycle limits; Duties, backing and fees.
findings.suggestedChange: Preserve this per-duty presentation in any wallet summary and pair it with the relevant continuation/close limitation when a duty remains.

findings.impact: High: issuer cannot identify actual policy that mints the app asset.
findings.observation: Inspector requires issuer policy/authenticated path; missing-work disclosure calls for actual policy enforcement. C2 policy mints proof claims, a different asset.
findings.evidence: Capped issuance role inspector, What this case still needs, FOLLOW THE VALUE; Evidence issuance route.
findings.suggestedChange: Say app-asset policy is unspecified/not demonstrated; label C2 flow proof-claim issuance and link exact app policy only if available.

findings.impact: Medium: “issuance” can mean app-asset supply or proof-claim output.
findings.observation: Evidence route title may sound like app-asset mint route; distinction requires following sections, though case explicitly clarifies claim token is separate.
findings.evidence: Capped issuance FOLLOW THE VALUE; Evidence issuance route.
findings.suggestedChange: Rename Evidence disclosure “Where proof claims are issued and checked” and link the app-asset policy gap.

findings.impact: Medium: conceptual handoff does not lead to actionable issuer integration.
findings.observation: No shipping SDK/integration; source command names are not executed here; proposed Web/transaction commands are not runnable here.
findings.evidence: Developer journey disclosure Current source commands & proposed interfaces.
findings.suggestedChange: Link supported issuer workflow if available, otherwise state no supported app-asset issuance workflow is shown.

findings.impact: A payer comparing the supplied section screenshot with the live worksheet can think the starting funding amount changed or that 112 is the source default.
findings.observation: The supplied worksheet screenshot shows “PROPOSED full-backing policy” selected with Escrow funding 112 CASH at the 35 payment. In a fresh isolated browser visit, “Source behavior (S12, not executed)” is selected with Escrow funding 110 CASH, Cash remaining 73, and a 2 CASH backing gap. The proposed button changes the live state to 112. Both states are clearly described once read, but the supplied screenshot does not identify itself as the proposed state.

evidence.freshBrowserDefault: #worksheet at 35; source mode; funding 110; cash remaining 73; duties 75; 2 CASH backing gap

findings.suggestedChange: Label the section screenshot as the proposed 112 state or update it to match the fresh page default; make the selected mode visible in any screenshot used as the worksheet preview.

findings.impact: Low; helps a reader compare the two selected financial examples while keeping units and obligations distinct.
findings.observation: Both examples provide useful case-specific arithmetic, but the comparison happens by switching cards. Loan servicing uses CASH debt/accrual/fee values; treasury uses separate A and B custody/duty values. I could follow each separately, but a compact comparison would make their different accounting roles easier to retain. This is a preference, not a behavior defect.
findings.evidence: Actions 0–3 in navigation.json; loan example and Treasury allocation screenshot.
findings.suggestedChange: Consider a small comparison recap with separate columns for cash flow/debt/fee and A/B custody/liabilities, retaining the existing warning that the cases are illustrations.

findings.impact: Low; leaves an economist unable to assess whether the treasury backing policy covers all costs.
findings.observation: Treasury allocation gives source custody and proposed liability backing but no fee quantity, asset or recipient. The shared disclosure says network fees are separate funding items, without assigning one to this example.
findings.evidence: Treasury “FOLLOW THE VALUE”; “Duties, backing and fees” disclosure; action 5.
findings.suggestedChange: If fees are intentionally outside this example, label the treasury arithmetic fee-exclusive. Otherwise show fee asset, recipient and amount separately from A/B liabilities.

findings.impact: Medium: a transaction builder needs a direct map from roles to transaction boundaries before implementing a builder.
findings.observation: The answer is spread across the role inspector, the long “Where proofs are checked: the issuance route” disclosure, the developer journey, and evidence disclosures. The route answer is precise about the proposed Issue/settlement split, but it is explicitly a source reading rather than observed behavior.
findings.evidence: screenshots/fee-accounting-inspector.png; “Where proofs are checked: the issuance route”; “Current source commands & proposed interfaces”.
findings.suggestedChange: Add a compact lifecycle diagram or table: owner intent signed → Issue proof checked and claim output created → settlement consumes claims and checks claimant signatures → validator effects/readback. Mark each stage with its evidence status and identify which stages are proposed, source-read, or not observed.

findings.impact: High for implementing a transaction builder: signer gathering and transaction assembly depend on exact signer placement.
findings.observation: The page says owner intents are signed before proving and claimants sign the settlement transaction, but does not show a transaction-by-transaction signer matrix or a complete build/submit/observe interface.
findings.evidence: “Where proofs are checked: the issuance route”; “Effects, allocation and authority”; “Current source commands & proposed interfaces”.
findings.suggestedChange: State the signer set by transaction (intent authorization, each Issue, settlement, reclaim if applicable), and label any missing or proposed mapping as unresolved.

findings.impact: High for determining when the builder can report success.
findings.observation: The page explicitly says transaction build/submit/observe families are proposals and that no on-chain transaction is recorded. It does not present an observed consumer acceptance or effect readback boundary.
findings.evidence: “Current source commands & proposed interfaces”; “What has actually been recorded”.
findings.suggestedChange: Show the intended acceptance/readback signal and distinguish local assembly, submission, ledger acceptance, effect observation, and completion; keep stages without evidence marked unobserved.

findings.impact: A keyboard visitor following the hero’s direct worksheet link first sees the proof-role illustration; reaching the amount control requires more scrolling and focus movement.
findings.observation: Activating ‘Inspect the invoice worksheet’ changed the fragment to #worksheet but the captured first view was the role diagram and inspector. The payment worksheet heading appeared below that view. The link works, but its destination is broader than its label suggests.
findings.evidence: navigation.json action 1; screenshots/worksheet-keyboard.png; after navigation the page showed #worksheet and the role board before the amount controls.
findings.suggestedChange: Point this link at the payment worksheet heading/control, or adjust its label to say it opens the combined explorer and worksheet area.

findings.impact: The amount the visitor just changed differs from the payment value shown in the adjacent role inspector, which can make the worksheet feel disconnected from its proof-role explanation.
findings.observation: ArrowRight changed the labeled Seller payment slider from 35 to 36 CASH, while the Payment arithmetic inspector continued to say payment 35 CASH and escrow debit 37 CASH. The page identifies the role as illustrative, but does not explain this mismatch at the interaction point.
findings.evidence: navigation.json action 2; screenshots/worksheet-keyboard.png shows the inspector’s 35 CASH and 37 CASH values; keyboard interaction log records slider value 36.
findings.suggestedChange: Update the inspector statement when the slider changes, or state beside the slider/inspector that the role statement is a fixed 35 CASH illustration.

findings.impact: On a 390×844 screen, selecting a role changes its selected card, but the explanation remains below the diagram and the full role list. The inspector heading begins near the bottom edge, so the tap gives little immediate confirmation about where the details went.
findings.observation: After selecting Pool arithmetic, the inspector heading was at y≈718 in the viewport; I needed a further scroll before the role description was readable.
findings.evidence: reached-role-inspector.png; inspector heading bounding box y=717.67 before scroll.
findings.suggestedChange: On small screens, move the inspector directly after the selected role card or scroll it into view when a role is selected.

findings.impact: The Explore header link is only about 39px wide at this viewport, although it is 44px high.
findings.observation: The small width makes the first header target feel less forgiving than the worksheet and case controls on a touch screen.
findings.evidence: Runtime bounding box for the Explore anchor: 39.05×44px at 390×844; mobile-top.png.
findings.suggestedChange: Give compact header links more horizontal padding on narrow screens.

findings.impact: Medium for a diligence reader trying to form a quick trust-boundary summary.
findings.observation: The explanations are present and mutually qualified, but answering the three diligence questions required opening multiple summaries across the Evidence section and joining technical labels such as T1/T2/T3 with the evidence-stage glossary.
findings.evidence: Evidence navigation plus Current maturity, Setup and keys, What ties a Strand to its step, Correspondence, Where proofs are checked, What has actually been recorded, and Source-reading scope disclosures; own reached-state screenshots.
findings.suggestedChange: Consider adding a compact at-a-glance map with three rows—setup, source/compiler correspondence, ledger acceptance—each linking to its detailed disclosure and stating the evidence stage. Keep the existing detail and ask Opus to review any security interpretation or revised security wording.

findings.impact: Low; it affects speed of orientation rather than whether the information can be found.
findings.observation: The Evidence nav label is easy to recognize and the explicit “OPEN,” “PROPOSED,” and “not observed onchain” wording is helpful. The long, dense maturity paragraph appears before the individual disclosures.
findings.evidence: Desktop top screenshot and observed #evidence section; mobile top screenshot reviewed for nav and opening layout.
findings.suggestedChange: I would prefer the three question headings near the start of Evidence, with the current maturity detail below them. Preserve the explicit stage labels.

findings.impact: A product lead cannot infer who should adopt the concept first or which user workflow anchors the roadmap.
findings.observation: The page presents contract and financial concepts but does not identify a primary audience. The hero promises an explicit financial-to-proof handoff, while the explorer says no concrete proof instances or producers exist.
findings.evidence: Hero audience and value copy; explorer section ‘Give every proof a defined job’ and selected-role inspector text. This is an observed omission from the inspected page, not evidence about users.
findings.suggestedChange: State the intended first audience and the concrete job this concept is meant to help them do.

findings.impact: A reader may not understand the maturity boundary or see the key distinction between a local evidence packet, a proposed concept, and a usable integration path without opening dense supporting copy.
findings.observation: The hero includes a concise caveat, but the expanded maturity disclosure contains a long paragraph with many identifiers and qualifications. The most decision-relevant facts are mixed with evidence labels and source-reading scope in one block.
findings.evidence: Visible hero disclosure state in screenshots/maturity-open.png and its expanded text: concept under review, S07/S08 evidence, no on-chain transaction, unestablished integration, and illustrative examples.
findings.suggestedChange: Keep the detailed evidence, while adding a short plain-language ‘today / proposed / not yet’ summary before the identifiers.

findings.impact: A clearer first-use cue would make the concept easier to explain to a stakeholder who has not read the page closely.
findings.observation: The hero's ‘Make the handoff from financial requirements to concrete proofs and the consuming script explicit’ is the clearest value statement, but it describes a design aim rather than a current capability.
findings.evidence: Hero paragraph and caveat immediately below the two calls to action.
findings.suggestedChange: Pair the design aim with one plain sentence saying that the current page is an interactive concept walkthrough and local arithmetic illustration.

questions.question: What API, library, or adapter does a Cardano DEX call to construct a Web and connect its Strands to the consuming script?
questions.whereItArose: “Explore a Web” and the Batched DEX orders case in the Web Explorer.
questions.answerLocation: The Explorer explains the intended mapping from claim specification to Strand and consuming script; “Current source commands & proposed interfaces” names future mori web assemble as a proposal.
questions.remainingClarification: There is no runnable Web API, DEX adapter, integration sample, or interface contract on this page. Which interface is actually implemented, and where can a developer use it?

questions.question: Which developer-facing commands exist today, and what do they do in a DEX workflow?
questions.whereItArose: “Current source commands & proposed interfaces” under Developer journey.
questions.answerLocation: It says the source README documents mori-k2 compile, inspect, setup, prove, and verify, and says the page did not execute them. It names mori obligations inspect, mori web assemble, and transaction build/submit/observe as future proposals.
questions.remainingClarification: The page does not link or reproduce the README instructions, nor map those commands to a working DEX example. I cannot tell from this page which parts are usable for this task.

questions.question: Are the three DEX roles three independent proofs that the application must produce?
questions.whereItArose: The DEX case’s illustrative role set.
questions.answerLocation: Explorer caption says roles are requirements, not three independent proof producers or concrete Strands; a native whole-execution proof may cover several arithmetic conditions.
questions.remainingClarification: What concrete producer and consumer interfaces implement this relationship in a supported deployment? The page marks them unestablished.

questions.question: Is this a deployed Cardano integration, and does selecting a role perform proof or transaction work?
questions.whereItArose: Hero description and interactive Web Explorer.
questions.answerLocation: Hero calls it a proposed Cardano concept and says general Web integration and onchain settlement are unestablished; role inspector says the omission control is explanatory, not a transaction action.
questions.remainingClarification: No live integration or runnable transaction path is demonstrated; this page gives no deployment or usage entrypoint.

questions.question: What exactly would I be approving as the asset owner, and what appears on the signing screen?
questions.whereItArose: While moving from the worksheet's arithmetic to an owner-facing wallet confirmation.
questions.answerLocation: Collapsed Effects, allocation and authority disclosure: V2 SOURCE READING lists per-asset gross_cap, fee_cap, net_floor, liability_cap, beneficiary, validity window, nonce and target predicate. The top maturity note says no signatures run on the page; the disclosure says no genuine intent signature is observed.
questions.remainingClarification: The page does not show a wallet approval screen, the exact human-readable intent presented to the owner, or which concrete signers and transaction effects would be requested in a real transaction. The V2 description is an uncompiled-source reading, not demonstrated wallet behavior.

questions.question: Is the 2 CASH fee the application fee or the network fee, and who pays each amount?
questions.whereItArose: The worksheet lists a 2 CASH Program fee while a wallet user normally needs to distinguish all outgoing amounts.
questions.answerLocation: Worksheet labels the 2 CASH amount Program fee and Fee recipient receives; Duties, backing and fees says a program-asset fee is not a network fee and names network fees as separate. Exact asset, opening costs & lifecycle limits lists network fees among costs outside the CASH worksheet.
questions.remainingClarification: No network fee estimate, fee asset/units, payer, or total wallet debit including network costs is shown. The 3 CASH buyer opening fee is separately described for source open(90,10), with gross buyer debit 113.

questions.question: After a 35 CASH partial payment, what is still owed, and can the reserve duty be returned at completion?
questions.whereItArose: The worksheet's gross-debit calculation and the separate reserve duty.
questions.answerLocation: Worksheet shows invoice duty 65, reserve duty 10, total duties 75 after payment 35 plus program fee 2; Exact asset, opening costs & lifecycle limits and Duties, backing and fees say the reserve duty persists after finish, no reserve-duty-return action exists, and nonzero duty blocks V2 Close.
questions.remainingClarification: The page says discharge or migration requires a program change but does not specify a supported wallet recovery path, responsible party, or timing. The Close condition is identified as an uncompiled-source reading.

questions.question: Does the proof itself mean that the payment was authorized or settled?
questions.whereItArose: The page's proof-oriented headline and transition from arithmetic to a proposed Web.
questions.answerLocation: Top page says no proofs, signatures or transactions run. Explorer says assembly is not proof verification, acceptance or settlement; role details separate proof arithmetic from actual signatures and validator enforcement. What a verifying proof shows says supplied bytes are not thereby authenticated ledger facts.
questions.remainingClarification: A concrete consumer and wallet signing-to-ledger sequence are not demonstrated, so the page does not provide a real approval or settlement walkthrough.

questions.question: Is the unused 700 below the cap debt?
questions.whereItArose: Capped issuance example, cap 1,000 and issue 300.
questions.answerLocation: FOLLOW THE VALUE explicitly says no debt is inferred from unissued capacity.
questions.remainingClarification: Any redemption/servicing duty is separate; case says define it separately.

questions.question: Which actual policy authorizes/mints the application asset under this cap?
questions.whereItArose: Supply arithmetic inspector and missing-work disclosure.
questions.answerLocation: Evidence names C2 claim policy for proof claims; case says those do not mint app asset.
questions.remainingClarification: No app-asset mint policy, issuer path or runnable implementation is identified.

questions.question: Can I use this handoff to issue the asset today?
questions.whereItArose: Developer journey and command disclosure.
questions.answerLocation: Page says no shipping SDK; future Web/transaction commands are proposals, not runnable here.
questions.remainingClarification: No issuer-specific mint interface is shown.

questions.question: Does proof-claim issuance mint the application asset?
questions.whereItArose: Evidence heading “Where proofs are checked: the issuance route.”
questions.answerLocation: Case FOLLOW THE VALUE says no; Evidence says C2 issues a claim output.
questions.remainingClarification: App-asset policy remains unspecified.

questions.question: After the example payment of 35 CASH and the 2 CASH fee, what remains owed?
questions.whereItArose: Worksheet shows seller receives 35 and fee recipient receives 2.
questions.answerLocation: Worksheet totals: invoice duty 65, reserve duty 10, total duties 75; nearby note says only the seller payment discharges invoice duty and the fee does not.
questions.remainingClarification: None for the one partial shown.

questions.question: Does S12 itself provide the 112 CASH funding, or is 112 a proposed change?
questions.whereItArose: Worksheet screenshot starts at proposed funding 112, while the fresh interactive page starts at source funding 110.
questions.answerLocation: Worksheet note and FAQ “Can S12 fund the escrow with 112?” say 112 is a proposed policy, not an S12 action; the source only enforces non-negative custody.
questions.remainingClarification: The supplied worksheet screenshot should identify that it shows the proposed state because it differs from the fresh browser default.

questions.question: Is the 2 CASH partial fee added to the 35 CASH payment, and is there also an opening fee?
questions.whereItArose: Worksheet separates Seller receives from Fee recipient receives and states gross escrow debit; the buyer opening cost is not in the main arithmetic card.
questions.answerLocation: Worksheet says gross escrow debit is 37 CASH for a 35 payment plus 2 fee. Open “Exact asset, opening costs & lifecycle limits” to find that source open separately charges the buyer 3 CASH and gives gross opening debit 113.
questions.remainingClarification: None after opening the disclosure; the 3 CASH opening fee is easy to miss if the reader only sees the green worksheet card.

questions.question: In loan servicing, does the 2 CASH fee repay debt, or does only the 35 CASH payment reduce the 105 CASH closing obligation?
questions.whereItArose: Comparing 105 opening-plus-accrual debt, 37 gross debit and 70 closing debt.
questions.answerLocation: Loan servicing “FOLLOW THE VALUE” gives the 35 repayment, 2 fee and 70 closing debt. The “Duties, backing and fees” disclosure says a program-asset fee is not debt repayment. The displayed arithmetic implies 35 reduces debt.
questions.remainingClarification: The case does not identify the fee asset/recipient in this exact loan example or show a separate debt-evolution equation.

questions.question: What period, rate, rounding and collateral/origination rules produce the 5 CASH accrual and govern collateral release?
questions.whereItArose: Loan servicing displays 100 + 5 = 105 and says collateral release needs its own policy.
questions.answerLocation: The loan servicing “What this case still needs” disclosure explicitly says to define period, rate, rounding and observation freshness; it also asks for separate origination and collateral policies.
questions.remainingClarification: Those model inputs and policies are not supplied.

questions.question: For treasury allocation, which amounts are required to stay in custody, which amounts are liabilities, and does an allocation discharge either duty?
questions.whereItArose: Comparing treasury case follow-the-value and Reserve accounting inspector.
questions.answerLocation: Treasury “FOLLOW THE VALUE” and Reserve accounting inspector: 23 A / 4 B source minimum custody; proposed backing 25 A / 10 B; creates 2 A and 6 B duties and discharges neither. rebate(amount) can discharge B rebate; S13 has no allocation_reserve discharge action.
questions.remainingClarification: The example identifies the two duties and a B rebate path, but does not specify a program action for clearing the 2 A allocation reserve duty.

questions.question: Are treasury fees included in its example amounts, and if so, what asset, recipient and amount apply?
questions.whereItArose: The loan case explicitly shows a 2 fee, while the treasury case reports A/B custody and duties.
questions.answerLocation: “Duties, backing and fees” says network fees and other funding items are separate; the Treasury allocation case does not state a fee amount or fee recipient.
questions.remainingClarification: Whether a treasury allocation has a program or network fee, its asset and recipient, and whether it is included in the proposed 25 A / 10 B backing.

questions.question: Does the 112 CASH worksheet establish source behavior or product execution?
questions.whereItArose: Worksheet toggle and its relationship to the selected examples.
questions.answerLocation: The worksheet labels the 112 view “PROPOSED full-backing policy”; its note says arithmetic only, not Moriarty execution, proof verification or settlement. “Sources & scope” identifies invoice open/partial/finish as source material.
questions.remainingClarification: None for the page’s stated scope.

questions.question: What does the prototype establish today about these financial examples?
questions.whereItArose: The examples look like financial flows with specific payment, debt, fee and backing quantities.
questions.answerLocation: “Current maturity · scoped local evidence” says every interactive example is an illustration, no on-chain transaction is recorded, and general Web integration, genuine intent authorization and on-chain settlement remain unestablished.
questions.remainingClarification: The page describes scoped local evidence for invoice partials, not evidence for loan servicing or treasury allocation.

questions.question: Are the three invoice role cards three separate proof producers or three existing proofs?
questions.whereItArose: The selected invoice case displays three required-role cards and “Illustrative set assembled.”
questions.answerLocation: Explorer caption and inspector: “Illustration of one proposed Web’s three required FUTURE proof-role specifications”; “not three independent proof producers”; the “What this case still needs” disclosure.
questions.remainingClarification: No additional clarification needed for the distinction; the page says a native whole-execution proof may cover several arithmetic conditions.

questions.question: What is the proposed Issue → consume sequence, and which signatures occur at each point?
questions.whereItArose: While tracing a builder’s transaction and witness preparation across the issuance-route disclosure.
questions.answerLocation: “Where proofs are checked: the issuance route” says one Issue per required Strand checks the proof and creates a claim output; settlement consumes claims, recomputes statements, and requires each claimant signature and token burn. It separately says owner intents are signed before proving. “Effects, allocation and authority” describes owner-intent fields.
questions.remainingClarification: The page does not give a concrete per-transaction signer set or say exactly which transaction carries the owner-intent signatures versus any other required authorizations. These are V2 source readings of uncompiled files, not observed behavior.

questions.question: What concrete ledger observation confirms settlement effects and completion?
questions.whereItArose: The proposed developer handoff includes readback/observe, while the route FAQ stops at a structural source description.
questions.answerLocation: “Current source commands & proposed interfaces” says transaction build/submit/observe families are proposals, not runnable commands here. “What has actually been recorded” says no on-chain transaction is recorded.
questions.remainingClarification: What actual consumer/validator acceptance, transaction submission, output/state readback, and completion/finality evidence will establish this stage for a supported target.

questions.question: Does the page’s 112 funding or reserve return belong to the S12 transaction?
questions.whereItArose: The payment arithmetic raises 112 as a proposed full-backing path and the case asks about reserve return.
questions.answerLocation: “Can S12 fund the escrow with 112?”, “Does finishing the invoice return the reserve?”, and “What this case still needs”.
questions.remainingClarification: The page says 112 funding and reserve-duty return are not S12 actions; no further clarification needed for this review.

questions.question: What does the page mean by a Web, a Strand, and a claim specification?

questions.answerLocation: The three nearby sections titled ‘A Web’, ‘A Strand’, and ‘A claim specification’ after the hero: a Web is the proposed script-bound collection required for a transition; a Strand is an individual proof with claim, statement, and binding metadata; a claim specification is a reusable assertion definition.
questions.remainingClarification: The page defines the concepts, but the illustrated roles are explicitly not concrete Strands.

questions.question: Does assembling the three roles mean proofs have been produced or verified?

questions.answerLocation: The note below the role diagram says the roles are future role specifications, not concrete Strands, proof instances, a verified set, or settlement; the status panel also says ‘Not proof verification, not acceptance, not settlement.’
questions.remainingClarification: None for this prototype walkthrough; no proof or settlement action is provided.

questions.question: Does changing Seller payment from 35 to 36 update the Payment arithmetic statement?

questions.remainingClarification: Please clarify whether the inspector should track the slider or whether the two figures are separate examples; if separate, label that relationship near the controls.

questions.question: Can I use this page as SDK instructions or run commands from it?

questions.answerLocation: The keyboard-opened ‘Can I use these as SDK instructions?’ disclosure says these are proposed learning stages, not shipping SDK methods or runnable commands.
questions.remainingClarification: The page points to a target-specific capability guide, but does not link a specific guide in this answer.

questions.question: Can I switch examples and see which proof roles belong to each one?

questions.remainingClarification: None for the interaction; all examples are described as proposed/illustrative.

questions.question: When I select a role, where do I read what that role means on a phone?
questions.whereItArose: After tapping Pool arithmetic in the mobile role list.
questions.answerLocation: “Inspect an illustrated role” panel after the diagram and role cards.

questions.question: Does the slider represent an executed payment, and what changes when I choose full backing?
questions.whereItArose: At the financial worksheet slider and funding-mode buttons.
questions.answerLocation: The worksheet calls itself independent local arithmetic; labels S12 as not executed and the 112 CASH funding as a proposed policy/program change.
questions.remainingClarification: None for this example. It explicitly says later partials need another fee allowance.

questions.question: What does a Web and a Strand mean, and what does this page establish today?
questions.whereItArose: The hero, Explorer, “What is a Strand?” disclosure, and “Current maturity · scoped local evidence” disclosure.
